label: Heart rate
hrpRisk: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations
canMeasureInSpace: Yes. This app estimates pulse from tiny color changes in your face on the webcam. On the ISS, crews have worn the Canadian Bio-Monitor smart shirt, which tracks heart pulse and the heart's electrical activity.
whyCheck: Low gravity and other spaceflight stressors can change the heart and blood vessels. Heart rate, blood pressure and breathing all affect each other, so heart rate gives an early look at how your circulation is adapting.
hazardEffect: Altered gravity can change the heart's shape and raise the risk of heart rhythm problems (arrhythmias) and blood clots. NASA says these risks grow on longer missions, and radiation may also affect the heart and blood vessels.
whenToEscalate: Tell the crew medical officer or flight surgeon if your reading stays yellow or turns red against your own baseline, especially with palpitations, dizziness or fainting. NASA lists heart rhythm problems among the cardiovascular risks.
prevention: Regular exercise and a healthy diet help crews keep their cardiovascular fitness. For Mars missions, NASA plans enhanced crew training for cardiovascular emergencies.
recommendedAction: Take today's reading at rest, in good light, at your usual time, and do your scheduled exercise session.

label: Blood pressure (systolic)
hrpRisk: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations
canMeasureInSpace: Yes. You enter the top (systolic) number from a cuff. ISS crew members measure their own blood pressure, and the CSA Bio-Monitor shirt can also track it.
whyCheck: In weightlessness, the fluid circulating in the body drops, so blood pressure runs lower than on Earth. Tracking it shows how your circulation is coping.
hazardEffect: Altered gravity deconditions the heart and lungs and lowers fluid volume. That can bring low blood pressure, which raises the chance of fainting at landing.
whenToEscalate: Tell the crew medical officer or flight surgeon if your reading stays yellow or turns red against your own baseline, or if you feel faint or lightheaded.
prevention: Exercise and a healthy diet support cardiovascular fitness. Before landing, lower-body compression garments and drinking plenty of fluids help prevent low blood pressure.
recommendedAction: Measure seated and rested, the same way each day, and log it right away.

label: Blood pressure (diastolic)
hrpRisk: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations
canMeasureInSpace: Yes. You enter the bottom (diastolic) number from the same cuff reading. ISS crew members take their own blood pressure readings as part of heart-health monitoring.
whyCheck: Blood pressure and heart rate affect each other, and weightlessness lowers the fluid in your circulation. Tracking both numbers gives a fuller picture of how your heart and blood vessels are adapting.
hazardEffect: Low-gravity conditions and other spaceflight stressors can alter the heart and blood vessels. NASA links this to low blood pressure and a higher chance of fainting at landing.
whenToEscalate: Tell the crew medical officer or flight surgeon if your reading stays yellow or turns red against your own baseline, or if you feel faint or dizzy.
prevention: Exercise and a healthy diet help maintain cardiovascular fitness. Compression garments and extra fluids before landing help prevent low blood pressure.
recommendedAction: Log both cuff numbers from the same reading, taken at rest at your usual time.

label: Blink rate
hrpRisk: Risk of Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules
canMeasureInSpace: Yes. The app counts blinks per minute from webcam face landmarks. NASA fatigue research tracks eye movements with oculomotor tests and measures sleep with wrist-worn actigraphy.
whyCheck: Researchers use blink rate as a sign of fatigue. In one study it rose as fatigue built up during a task. It is only a rough proxy, not a diagnosis.
hazardEffect: Crews on the ISS see 16 sunrises and sunsets a day. Noise, light and work overload in the closed cabin also disrupt sleep and can increase fatigue.
whenToEscalate: If your reading keeps coming back yellow or red against your own baseline, or you notice lapses of attention or mistakes, tell the crew medical officer or flight surgeon.
prevention: Protect your sleep period with light blockers, an eye mask and earplugs. Follow the LED lighting schedule that simulates Earth's day-night cycle.
recommendedAction: Retest with your whole face in view: head movement and glasses can spoil camera readings. If it is still off-baseline, protect tonight's full sleep period.

label: Eyelid closure
hrpRisk: Risk of Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules
canMeasureInSpace: Yes. The app uses the webcam to estimate the share of time your eyes are mostly closed (a PERCLOS-style measure). PERCLOS is already built into devices such as network cameras.
whyCheck: PERCLOS is a well-studied drowsiness measure. Eyelid closure measures consistently go up after long periods awake or at times of low body-clock alertness.
hazardEffect: Irregular light-dark cycles in orbit can throw your body clock out of step with your schedule. That mismatch lowers alertness and performance.
whenToEscalate: Check in with the crew medical officer or flight surgeon if you get a yellow or red result against your baseline, especially before critical tasks. Sleep loss can cause errors in judgment.
prevention: Keep a regular sleep schedule and use the pre-sleep and alertness lighting settings. NASA is studying blue-enriched light as a way to recover alertness after waking.
recommendedAction: Retest with your face fully in the camera's view. If the reading is still high, tell your crewmates before you start any critical task.

label: Sleep duration
hrpRisk: Risk of Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules
canMeasureInSpace: Yes. The app uses the hours you log. NASA measures crew sleep with wrist-worn actigraphy devices and questionnaires.
whyCheck: Sleep is vital for physical and mental health, thinking and work performance. Astronauts average only about six hours of sleep in space, which is less than recommended.
hazardEffect: Many things cut sleep short in flight: microgravity, raised CO2, light, noise, temperature, lack of privacy, heavy workload and shifting schedules.
whenToEscalate: Repeated yellow or red nights against your baseline add up to sleep debt, which affects health, concentration and decisions. Report it to the crew medical officer or flight surgeon.
prevention: Sleep in a dedicated space that is cool, quiet and dark, with restraints. Plan work-rest schedules that leave enough time to sleep.
recommendedAction: Protect tonight's full scheduled sleep period. The only way to pay back sleep debt is good-quality sleep.

label: Sleep quality
hrpRisk: Risk of Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules
canMeasureInSpace: Yes. You rate your sleep from 0 to 10 in the app. NASA also uses sleep questionnaires together with wrist actigraphy.
whyCheck: Peak performance needs both enough sleep and good-quality sleep. Poor sleep affects attention, memory and mood.
hazardEffect: Noise, temperature, vibration and light all disturb sleep in space. Some crew members feel like they are falling unless they are strapped in snugly.
whenToEscalate: If your rating stays yellow or red against your baseline, raise it with the crew medical officer. Sleep loss can lead to depressive symptoms and anxiety.
prevention: Control your sleep environment with earplugs, an eye mask, light blockers and bedding restraints. Use dim light with less blue in it before sleep.
recommendedAction: Tonight, strap your sleeping bag in snugly and use an eye mask and earplugs.

label: Mood
hrpRisk: Risk of Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders
canMeasureInSpace: Yes. You rate your mood from 0 to 10 in the app. In flight, NASA crews take a monthly cognitive test compared with their preflight baseline (WinSCAT) and have private psychological conferences.
whyCheck: Stress, depression and anxiety can happen in spaceflight. Spotting changes early can help stop distress from developing into a psychiatric disorder.
hazardEffect: Isolation, radiation, distance from Earth and other stressors can take a toll on mental health. The risk is greater on longer missions that go farther from Earth.
whenToEscalate: If your mood trends yellow or red below your own baseline, or you find yourself pulling away from the crew, ask for a private talk with the flight surgeon or psychological support team.
prevention: Use the support NASA provides: private psychological and family conferences, crew care packages, movies and books. Good sleep also protects mood.
recommendedAction: Schedule a call with family or friends, or set aside time for Earth photography or journaling.

label: Stress
hrpRisk: Risk of Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders
canMeasureInSpace: Yes. You rate your stress from 0 to 10 in the app. NASA provides in-flight psychological monitoring and private psychological conferences.
whyCheck: Spaceflight comes with its own unique stressors. Stress that goes unnoticed or unmanaged can lower performance and lead to behavioral health problems.
hazardEffect: NASA lists confinement, lack of privacy, bursts of heavy workload, limited contact with home and the lack of a rescue option as stressors.
whenToEscalate: If your stress stays yellow or red against your baseline, or it is hurting your sleep or teamwork, ask for a private psychological conference.
prevention: Training in stress management and small-group living helps. So do personal control over light, noise and temperature, private space and a balanced workload.
recommendedAction: Take a short break to journal or photograph Earth. NASA notes both help astronauts manage stress.

label: Amsler grid distortion
hrpRisk: Risk of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS)
canMeasureInSpace: Yes. The app shows an on-screen Amsler grid for each eye. NASA long-duration crews do Amsler grid tests in flight, along with visual acuity, fundoscopy, ultrasound and OCT.
whyCheck: SANS can cause folds in the retina. Folds near the center of vision can make what you see look distorted or less sharp, so new wavy or missing areas matter.
hazardEffect: In weightlessness, body fluids shift toward the head, and this is the most likely cause of SANS. The risk is higher on longer missions.
whenToEscalate: Report any new distortion, or any yellow or red result against your baseline, to the flight surgeon. Extra eye tests such as OCT can be done whenever there is a medical reason.
prevention: Nothing is proven to prevent SANS yet. Crews are given B vitamins, which are being studied, and thigh cuffs and lower body negative pressure are being considered to reduce fluid shift.
recommendedAction: Test each eye separately, and report any new wavy or missing area to the crew medical officer.

label: Near visual acuity
hrpRisk: Risk of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS)
canMeasureInSpace: Yes. The app uses an on-screen tumbling-E test. NASA tests visual acuity before, during and after flight, including near vision before launch.
whyCheck: SANS can shift the eye toward farsightedness. That can cause eyestrain or blurry near vision and affect how well you do tasks.
hazardEffect: Fluid shifting toward the head in weightlessness can flatten the back of the eye and make you more farsighted. The risk to vision grows the longer you are in space.
whenToEscalate: Report a yellow or red drop against your own baseline, or new blurry near vision, to the flight surgeon so your eyes can be examined.
prevention: Every crew member flies with at least three pairs of prescription glasses of different strengths (Space Anticipation Glasses) to make up for vision shifts.
recommendedAction: If close-up text looks blurry, switch to a stronger spare pair of glasses as directed and tell the crew medical officer.

label: Exercise
hrpRisk: Risk of Spaceflight-Induced Bone Changes; Risk of Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness
canMeasureInSpace: You type in your minutes. On the ISS, crews exercise on ARED (weightlifting), the T2 treadmill and the CEVIS cycle, and researchers monitor the sessions.
whyCheck: Without Earth's gravity, bone and muscle get smaller and weaker. NASA says exercise is critical for keeping bones and muscles healthy in space.
hazardEffect: Altered gravity: bones lose about 1-1.5% density per month without countermeasures. Distance: future Moon/Mars craft will have less room for exercise gear. Weaker fitness raises fall risk when landing on a new world.
whenToEscalate: Yellow or red means you are well below your own usual minutes. If it stays low, tell your crew medical officer or flight surgeon, since exercise plans are adjusted using health data.
prevention: Daily resistance plus aerobic exercise (ISS crews average about two hours a day). NASA also studies bone medication (bisphosphonates) and tracks bone density before and after flight.
recommendedAction: Fit in your scheduled resistance and aerobic session today and log the minutes.

label: Body temperature
hrpRisk: Risk of Altered Immune System Responses
canMeasureInSpace: Yes. You enter a thermometer reading. In an ISS study, researchers tracked astronauts' core temperature with a forehead sensor that combines skin-temperature and heat-flux sensing.
whyCheck: Even small rises in core body temperature can impair physical and cognitive performance. A rise can also go along with infection, and ISS astronauts have reported infections.
hazardEffect: On long ISS missions, resting core temperature rose by about 1 °C over 2.5 months. During exercise it rose higher and faster than on Earth. Radiation, microgravity and poor sleep can also alter the immune system.
whenToEscalate: Tell the crew medical officer or flight surgeon if your temperature stays yellow or turns red against your own baseline, especially with signs of infection, a rash or cold sores.
prevention: Before launch, crews limit exposure to large groups for two weeks to lower infection risk. Getting good sleep supports immune health.
recommendedAction: Take your temperature at rest, not right after exercise, at the same time each day.

label: Radiation dose
hrpRisk: Risk of Radiation-Induced Cancers
canMeasureInSpace: Yes. The ISS carries instruments that measure radiation exposure, and Artemis II crews wear personal crew active dosimeters. In this app the dose is simulated by replaying a real solar event from NASA DONKI.
whyCheck: Astronauts get more radiation in space than on Earth, which can lead to certain cancers. It may also affect the heart, blood vessels and eyes, and cause cognitive or performance problems during a mission.
hazardEffect: Earth's magnetosphere shields the planet from most space radiation, but Moon and Mars missions go beyond it. Solar particle events can raise radiation levels inside the spacecraft.
whenToEscalate: Follow flight control and onboard radiation alarms right away. For Artemis II, a lower dose level prompts caution and closer monitoring, and a higher threshold triggers a recommendation to take shelter.
prevention: Ground teams watch the Sun around the clock. Crews train to rearrange stowed gear to add shielding mass and can shelter in Orion's storm shelter, and NASA is developing better shielding and protective medicines.
recommendedAction: Review where your spacecraft's shelter area is and how to rearrange gear for shielding, and wear your dosimeter if you have one.

label: Symptom report
hrpRisk: Risk of Adverse Health Outcomes and Decrements in Performance due to Inflight Medical Conditions
canMeasureInSpace: Yes. It is a self-report checklist that needs no equipment. NASA says every human spaceflight needs some in-mission medical support, and the ISS medical kit is basic, so your own report matters.
whyCheck: Many spaceflight problems show up first as symptoms. Examples include motion sickness, head congestion from fluid shifts, rashes, sleep loss and changes in mood or morale.
hazardEffect: Altered gravity can cause motion sickness and head congestion. Isolation and confinement can bring anxiety or depression. Irregular light cycles disrupt sleep, and space stressors can trigger rashes, allergies or cold sores.
whenToEscalate: Tell the crew medical officer or flight surgeon about new or worsening symptoms, especially fainting, confusion, headaches, vision changes, rashes or signs of infection, or if the checklist shows yellow or red against your baseline.
prevention: Use the lighting schedule that mimics Earth's day-night cycle, take your scheduled time for rest and self-care, and keep up regular contact with family and medical staff.
recommendedAction: Fill in the checklist honestly today. If anything is new or worse, write a short note in your journal and share it with the crew medical officer.

label: Blood sugar
hrpRisk: Risk of Inadequate Food and Nutrition
canMeasureInSpace: You type in the reading from a glucometer.
whyCheck: NASA notes that microgravity can alter insulin sensitivity and hormone levels early in flight, and that eating less than needed is common.
hazardEffect: Altered gravity: early metabolic changes, including altered insulin sensitivity. Fluid shifts and motion sickness can cut appetite, lowering food intake in the first days.
whenToEscalate: Yellow or red means today's value is far from your own baseline. Recheck, and if it stays off, contact your crew medical officer or flight surgeon.
prevention: Eat your planned meals so you meet your energy needs. NASA plans crew days with set meal times because skipped meals lead to undernourishment.
recommendedAction: Eat your scheduled meals today and log your intake alongside this reading.

label: Digestive comfort
hrpRisk: Risk of Host-Microorganism Interactions
canMeasureInSpace: You rate your comfort on a 0-10 slider. NASA tracks crew microbes in other ways, such as swabs from station surfaces.
whyCheck: Gut microbes change in space. In the Twins Study, Scott Kelly's gut flora was profoundly different in flight, then returned to normal after landing.
hazardEffect: Closed environment: microbes change and pass more easily between people. Altered gravity: fluid shifts slow stomach motility, and nausea or diarrhea are common in the first days. Prepackaged food may shift gut bacteria.
whenToEscalate: Yellow or red means you feel much worse than your usual. Report ongoing nausea, vomiting or diarrhea to your crew medical officer or flight surgeon: NASA warns these can cause dehydration.
prevention: Drink enough fluid and eat fiber, which NASA requires to support gut function. Medications for motion sickness and stool softeners or laxatives are on board if needed.
recommendedAction: Drink water steadily through the day and choose a fiber-containing food at your next meal.

label: Appetite
hrpRisk: Risk of Inadequate Food and Nutrition
canMeasureInSpace: You rate your appetite on a 0-10 slider. On the ISS, the ISS FIT tablet app lets crews see in real time how close they are to their daily nutrition needs.
whyCheck: Astronauts often don't eat enough in flight and can lose weight. Scott Kelly ate about 30% fewer calories than expected during his year in space.
hazardEffect: Altered gravity: fluid shifts and motion sickness reduce appetite early on, and taste or smell may change. Closed environment: trash and waste odors can lower appetite. Isolation: tiring of the same menu.
whenToEscalate: Yellow or red means your appetite is far below your usual. If it lasts, tell your crew medical officer or flight surgeon. Intake data are reviewed weekly and reported to the flight surgeon.
prevention: Varied menus, personal food choices and condiments (some crew prefer spicier food). Crew days include time for meals, including dining together as a team.
recommendedAction: Add a condiment or a favorite item to your next meal and eat it with your crewmates.

label: Body mass
hrpRisk: Risk of Inadequate Food and Nutrition
canMeasureInSpace: You type in your mass. Scales don't work in orbit, so the ISS SLAMMD device applies a known force and uses your acceleration to calculate your mass.
whyCheck: NASA monitors body mass in flight because under-eating causes weight loss. Poor intake in space has led to bone and muscle loss and weaker immune function.
hazardEffect: Altered gravity: bone and muscle loss. Distance: few resupply options, so food must last years. Closed environment and isolation: odors and menu fatigue cut intake. Scott Kelly lost 7% of body mass in a year.
whenToEscalate: Yellow or red means your mass is well away from your own baseline. A steady drop is worth raising with your crew medical officer or flight surgeon.
prevention: Eat enough to hold your weight: NASA sets energy needs individually from age, sex, mass and height. Real-time intake tracking and extra food choices help crews eat enough.
recommendedAction: Weigh in at your usual time and check whether you ate all your planned meals yesterday.

label: Bowel movements
hrpRisk: Risk of Host-Microorganism Interactions
canMeasureInSpace: You log how many times per day.
whyCheck: Some crew get constipation from bowel changes in microgravity, and diarrhea can occur in the first days. Gut microbes also shift during flight.
hazardEffect: Altered gravity: bowel changes and constipation. Closed environment: microbes in waste and hygiene areas can cause stomach illness, and microbes pass between crew more easily. Prepackaged food may shift gut bacteria.
whenToEscalate: Yellow or red means your count is far from your usual. Report ongoing diarrhea or no movements for a while to your crew medical officer or flight surgeon, since diarrhea can lead to dehydration.
prevention: NASA treats constipation with fluid and dietary fiber; stool softeners and laxatives are available if needed. Fiber requirements are set to help maintain gut function.
recommendedAction: Drink water through the day and include a high-fiber food at your next meal.

label: Water intake
hrpRisk: Risk of Inadequate Food and Nutrition
canMeasureInSpace: Yes: log each drink on the Log screen. NASA monitors what crews take in and sets a daily fluid requirement for exploration missions.
whyCheck: NASA's exploration requirement is 32 mL of fluid per kg of body mass a day, food and drinks together, and at least 2.1 L for women or 2.5 L for men.
hazardEffect: In weightlessness, fluid shifts toward the head can make your body think it has extra fluid, so you may drink less than you need.
whenToEscalate: If your daily total falls below your own usual (yellow or red), or vomiting or diarrhea stop you keeping fluids down, tell the crew medical officer.
prevention: Drink on purpose rather than waiting to feel thirsty, especially if you feel sick.
recommendedAction: Log your next drink now, and drink on purpose through the day.

label: Meals eaten
hrpRisk: Risk of Inadequate Food and Nutrition
canMeasureInSpace: Yes: mark each meal on the Log screen. NASA monitors crew food intake and body mass in flight.
whyCheck: Astronauts often do not eat enough in flight and can lose weight. Skipped meals lead to undernourishment.
hazardEffect: On a spacecraft the body cannot make vitamin D, so food has to supply what sunlight would on Earth, and crews tend to under-eat.
whenToEscalate: If meals eaten fall below your own usual (yellow or red), or your body mass keeps dropping, tell the crew medical officer.
prevention: Keep the meal times in the crew schedule. NASA plans crew days with time for meals, including eating together as a team.
recommendedAction: Don't skip your next meal: eat it at the scheduled time, with the crew if you can.

label: Reaction time
hrpRisk: Risk of Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules
canMeasureInSpace: Yes. Astronauts on the ISS have used the Reaction Self Test, a 3-minute reaction-time test on a computer.
whyCheck: Reaction time tracks alertness. It slows with sleep loss, long time awake and body-clock disruption, and practice barely changes it.
hazardEffect: Irregular light-dark cycles, heavy workload and isolation can disrupt sleep. In ISS astronauts, sleeping under 6 hours was linked to slower responses.
whenToEscalate: If your median time is slower than your own baseline (yellow), or stays slow or you miss many taps (red), tell your crew surgeon, especially after short sleep.
prevention: Protect your sleep. Station lights simulate Earth's day-night cycle, and crews get set time for rest and self-care. Longer sleep was linked to better performance.
recommendedAction: Protect tonight's sleep, retest later, and report a slow trend to your crew surgeon.
